papers.title: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophile phenotyping by measuring metabolic byproduct formation in microplates
papers.abstract: Chemolithoautotrophic acidophiles can support several low-pH biotechnologies, but their phenotyping remains limited by throughput and inconsistent methods. This study used an assay to monitor metabolic byproduct formation using absorbance indicators in static, oxic cultures in 96-well microplates. In abiotic experiments, ferric iron and/or pH measurements from 51 microplates containing simulant solutions span total iron concentrations of 0–1 M, pH 0.3–7.0, and incubation temperatures of 4–75 °C. Of these, 30 microplates tested different UV-transparency and gas-permeable membrane configurations. Another 12 microplates tested indicator compatibility with growth media containing ferrous iron and (in)soluble sulfur substrates. Biological experiments measured 438 microplates containing Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans ATCC 23270, Acidithiobacillus thiooxidans ATCC 19377, or Leptospirillum ferriphilum DSM 14647 with chemical additives across 1,400 concentration conditions, yielding 142,038 time-course points, including abiotic controls. Measurements of apparent substrate oxidation and/or growth from 96 culture tubes and 99 shake flasks provide context for microplate observations. The miniaturized assay and this dataset may be useful for microbiology, (critical-mineral) biotechnology development, and synthetic biology.

papers.title: Redesigning the bacterial envelope: Multi-layered genetic strategies for outer membrane vesicle production.
papers.abstract: Bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are promising nanoplatforms for therapeutics, vaccines, and bioengineering; however, their industrial translation is constrained by low native yields and strain-dependent heterogeneity. Although static genetic knockouts can enhance vesicle shedding, they often provoke envelope fragility, premature cell lysis, and downstream contamination-creating a severe trade-off between vesicle yield and host cellular fitness. This review systematically outlines genetic strategies to optimise OMV yield, cargo selectivity, and biosafety across four biophysical dimensions: outer membrane layer remodelling, periplasmic waste accumulation and turgor stress, outer membrane-peptidoglycan tether disruption, and multi-layered combinatorial engineering. For each dimension, the molecular mechanisms, comparative merits, and operational bottlenecks are analysed alongside representative biomedical and industrial applications. Finally, we discuss autonomous dynamic circuits for mitigating yield-fitness trade-offs and the prospective role of artificial intelligence (AI)-guided systems design, which remains contingent on suitable datasets and experimental validation. We further consider chassis diversification and standardised orthogonal phenotyping as complementary directions for advancing OMV biomanufacturing. Harnessing these integrated synthetic biology toolkits may facilitate the development of robust and scalable OMV biomanufacturing platforms.

papers.title: Assessing soluble and insoluble calcium sources for growth, biofilm formation, and biomineralization in Bacillus subtilis .
papers.abstract: Biofilms formed by soil microbes hold immense potential for bioremediation, carbon dioxide sequestration, and the development of sustainable cementitious materials. However, quantifying the complex temporal coupling among bacterial growth, extracellular matrix (ECM) production, and mineralization dynamics remains challenging because these processes are inherently non-linear and high-throughput assays introduce signal noise. To address this, we utilized an automated kinetic framework to evaluate the biomineralization competence of Bacillus subtilis under varying calcium regimes. Our results demonstrate that calcium carbonate promotes microbial growth as effectively as soluble calcium acetate, indicating that B. subtilis actively solubilizes the crystalline powder. Despite this growth efficacy, calcium carbonate was an inadequate source for macro-calcite production compared to organic salts. By quantifying expression from the sinI promoter, which initiates SinI production to activate matrix synthesis, we suggested that calcium-acetate-driven ECM expression significantly enhances the structural template required for robust biomineralization. Kinetic expression analysis and consolidation assays indicate that overproduced ECM partially mitigates crystalline calcite growth defects, offering a baseline for utilizing mineral-rich construction waste.IMPORTANCEBiomineralization in Bacillus subtilis has been studied as a potential avenue for developing engineered living materials (ELMs). However, organic calcium salts, such as calcium acetate and calcium lactate, typically yield higher bioconversion efficiencies than certain inorganic sources often used in construction. This advantage has been largely attributed to the metabolic utilization of the organic anion as a carbon source, thereby promoting local alkalinity. Here, our experiments indicate that this limitation is influenced by structural and regulatory constraints rather than purely chemical barriers. Moreover, we explored a targeted synthetic biology approach to address this by genetically decoupling matrix production from native environmental sensing, thereby engineering strains with increased matrix production that can partially overcome the limitations of non-inductive substrates. This approach can contribute to sustainable construction technologies, moving toward actively programmed ELMs.

papers.title: The Signal Peptide-like Sequence SP DrwH Mediates Membrane Targeting of DrwH and Confers Heterologous Toxicity toward the Escherichia coli Cell Envelope
papers.abstract: Abstract The subcellular localization of bacterial proteins depends on targeting sequences such as signal peptides. Whether signal peptide‑like motifs can be recognized to exert biological functions across species remains poorly understood. Here we characterized SP DrwH , an N‑terminal signal peptide‑like sequence of hydrophobic protein DrwH from Deinococcus radiodurans . Recombinant Escherichia coli BL21 strains producing full‑length DrwH, SP DrwH ‑deleted ΔSP mutant and their EGFP fusions were constructed for heterologous overexpression. Bioinformatic analysis predicted that conserved SP DrwH folds into an amphipathic α‑helix. Confocal microscopy verified that SP DrwH mediates DrwH targeting to the E. coli cell envelope. Full‑length DrwH triggered sequential outer‑to‑inner membrane disruption and severe host cytotoxicity, whereas the ΔSP mutant showed negligible damage phenotypes. Our results demonstrate that SP DrwH acts as a functional heterologous membrane‑targeting signal and confers DrwH‑associated cytotoxicity toward the bacterial cell envelope. This work expands our understanding of cross‑host recognition of extremophile‑derived targeting elements and inspires the development of minimal synthetic‑biology membrane‑targeting tools. Our findings lay a solid foundation for further mechanistic investigations of signal peptide‑like motifs from radiation‑resistant microorganisms.

papers.title: Moss is more: The moss Physcomitrium patens as an ideal chassis for plant synthetic biology.
papers.abstract: Physcomitrium patens, commonly known as the spreading earthmoss or Physco, has gained increasing attention as a chassis for synthetic biology in plants. This review explores its advantages over flowering plants traditionally used more often for biotechnology, such as Arabidopsis thaliana and maize, including shorter life cycles and ease to handle experimentally, being haploid, and much higher efficiency for integration of transgenes into its genome by homologous recombination. In addition, Physco's ability to maintain episomes also introduces an additional possibility for transgene expression and manipulation. With these advantageous traits, Physco has already been used for synthetic genomes, recombinant protein production, metabolic engineering and artificial organelle engineering. These applications have been enabled by various toolkits developed for construction of transformation cassettes, DNA and RNA editing, as well as different reporters to allow microscopy imaging or quantification of gene expression. While Physco does have limitations, such as its high number of duplicated genes which can present issues when tweaking of native genes is involved, these certainly do not prevent Physco becoming a useful synthetic biology model for further applications on Earth and future space explorations.

papers.title: Structure and function of iron-sulfur cluster enzymes used in isoprenoid biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: Bioproducts and bioplastics produced from microbes provide a sustainable alternative to fossil fuel derived products. In particular, isoprenoids are chemically suitable for production of various value-added products as well as biofuel as an alternative to fossil fuel derived products. Isoprenoid precursors are synthesized through the mevalonic acid pathway or the methyl erythritol phosphate pathway. Iron sulfur cluster containing enzymes IspG (4-hydroxy-3-methylbut-2-enyl diphosphate synthase) and IspH (4-hydroxy-3-methylbut-2-enyl diphosphate reductase) are the key bottleneck steps in the metabolic engineering of the methyl erythritol phosphate pathway for production of isoprenoid precursors. In this mini review, we summarize the previous reports on the structure and catalytic activity of both IspG and IspH enzymes. We also briefly describe on the biotechnological potential of these iron sulfur cluster containing enzymes of the methyl erythritol phosphate pathway.

papers.title: Construction of cell factories, and multi-enzymatic and chemoenzymatic cascades to enable the efficient production of alkaloids.
papers.abstract: Covering: up to 2025Alkaloids constitute an invaluable reservoir for pharmaceutical discovery. However, their therapeutic development has long been constrained by the inefficiencies of plant extraction, as well as the economic impracticality of total chemical synthesis. In recent years, biomanufacturing has emerged as a transformative paradigm, enabling sustainable and scalable access to these complex molecules. This review provides an overview of the pivotal advances in alkaloid biosynthesis, delineated across de novo biosynthesis in prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems, concise multi-enzyme cascades, and chemoenzymatic synthesis. By discussing these pioneering examples, analyzing the strategic lessons, inherent limitations, and corresponding solutions for these platforms, this review illuminates how synthetic biology and biocatalysis are collectively reshaping the landscape of alkaloid production and paving the way for their expanded pharmaceutical applications.

papers.title: A validated sfGFP fluorescence assay to monitor Escherichia coli extract productivity for cell- free biomanufacturing
papers.abstract: Abstract Cell-free protein synthesis represents a rapidly developing class of manufacturing technologies reported to enable rapid, scalable, decentralized, and versatile protein production for drug products. However, the batch-to-batch variability of the cell extract raw material used for the cell-free reaction may affect the production consistency and product quality. Therefore, we developed and validated an in vitro superfolder green fluorescent protein (sfGFP) productivity assay to quantify and compare the protein-synthesis output of Escherichia coli (E. coli) –derived cell extract batches for suitability prior to their use in establishing a cell-free manufacturing platform. Here, we report a validated quantitative fluorometric assay that is fit-for-purpose for monitoring batch-to-batch variation in extract productivity. This method was evaluated following International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) Q2(R2) and Q14 guidelines to support reproducibility and comparability across laboratories. Assay performance was assessed for specificity, linearity, limit of detection, limit of quantitation, accuracy, robustness, and precision. The assay exhibited a working range of (6.25 to 200) mg/L for sfGFP produced by the cell free reaction with linearity (R² ≥ 0.99) and intermediate precision ( in vitro sfGFP assay to characterize extract productivity and to inform strategies for monitoring extract performance in E. coli cell-free manufacturing workflows.

papers.title: Fermentable dietary fiber controls blood pressure by lowering large intestinal pH and activating the proton-sensing receptor GPR65.
papers.abstract: High blood pressure (BP) is the most common cause of death globally due to increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Fermentable dietary fibers regulate BP through gut microbial production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), acidic metabolites. How SCFAs regulate BP remains unclear. Here we show that, in a phenome-wide association study, the proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptor GPR65 gene is associated with human hypertension and cardiorenal phenotypes. Fermentable dietary fibers, delivered as a type 2 resistant starch (RS2), regulated luminal and interstitial tissue pH in the large intestine through gut microbial SCFA production in mice. High RS2 intake reduced pH, increased cAMP production via GPR65 signaling and CREB phosphorylation, and restricted the release of pro-hypertensive inflammatory cytokines by CD8+ T cells. Gpr65-/- mice spontaneously developed hypertension, cardiac and renal hypertrophy, and fibrosis. The benefits of a high-RS2 diet, which prevented these effects, were reduced in Gpr65-/- mice. Adoptive transfers revealed that GPR65 deficiency in CD8+ T cells explained this phenotype.

papers.title: Continuous Concentration of an Enveloped Virus Using Multi-Pass Tangential Flow Filtration.
papers.abstract: Continuous biomanufacturing often offers increased productivity and reduced capital costs over batch processing. However, the concentration of biomolecules, a critical step for reducing volumetric load, remains a challenge. While single-pass tangential flow filtration (SPTFF) is designed for continuous workflows, the low feed flow rates often lead to membrane fouling and limited operational stability. In this study, we explore a continuous tangential flow filtration (cTFF) configuration as a robust alternative. The cTFF design utilizes a high flow rate circulation loop with a continuous input and output from the loop. This design decouples membrane crossflow velocity from the overall volumetric throughput, providing increased shear rates to minimize fouling, while maintaining continuous flows into and out of the system. Suid herpesvirus 1 (SuHV) was used as a surrogate enveloped virus to determine an operational space to achieve high recovery without viral titer loss. The configuration was subsequently integrated into a continuous production line for influenza virus-like particles (IA VLPs). The cTFF achieved an 8X volumetric concentration and maintained steady-state operation for 21 h. cTFF bridges the gap between the operational robustness of traditional batch recirculating TFF and the need for continuous bioprocessing, providing a scalable solution for continuous concentration.

papers.title: Gene identity, not recoding strategy, determines the fitness cost of synonymous recoding in bacteriophage ΦX174
papers.abstract: Synthetic biology allows for the synthesis of genomes from scratch. Although technically achievable, our abilities in designing genomes that result in live organisms are in their infancy. One important consideration is synonymous codon usage bias, which is present in most organisms and shaped by selection for efficient translation. Many studies have edited the synonymous codon usage patterns of viruses with the goal of viral attenuation, but these studies almost always build a single construct per design, so we know little about how repeatable the effects of recoding are. We designed and built 111 synonymously recoded ΦX174 genomes, applying four recoding strategies at up to five levels of attenuation to each of three genes, with three independently designed replicates of most combinations. Which gene we recoded mattered considerably more than how we recoded it. Recoding genes for the major capsid protein F, the major spike protein G and the DNA pilot protein H in full, with the least-used synonym codons from E. coli cost 12.0, 10.8 and 5.9 doublings per hour, respectively. Recoding strategy per se had no detectable effect once the number of codons changed was accounted for. Predicted mRNA folding stability also had no measurable effect on fitness when tested in gene F, whose wildtype transcript is highly stable and could easily be destabilized with synonymous codon rearrangements. While the number of codons changed was correlated with the degree of attenuation, divergence between independently designed replicates increased as more codons were edited. Replicates of designs with small fitness effects varied little, while replicates of strongly attenuating designs diverged by several doublings per hour. The fitness outcome of large-scale genome recoding is therefore substantially unpredictable from the design variables alone: even among independently designed genomes receiving the same treatment, fitness can diverge substantially.

papers.title: Programmable functional RNA design with a virtual scientist.
papers.abstract: Programmable functional RNA design is central to synthetic biology and therapeutics, yet both human expertise and existing computational methods struggle to directly program the three-dimensional structures that govern function. Here we introduce RhoAgent, an agentic system that designs RNA candidates and iteratively refines them using experimental feedback. RhoAgent uses RDiff, a diffusion-based generative tool conditioned on base interactions and functional motifs. First, we validate RhoAgent by generating diverse and active ribozymes with only 40-70% sequence similarity to their wild-type counterparts. Second, we enhance the cleavage efficiency of the structurally uncharacterized hovlinc ribozyme by up to sixfold relative to the human-expert-truncated construct. Furthermore, RhoAgent generates a fluorogenic aptamer scaffold that improves fluorescence by 230% relative to the wild-type aptamer. Finally, we design three-dimensional scaffolds that spatially position two distinct functional cores, creating aptamer-based Förster resonance energy transfer systems. This design overcomes a key barrier in compositional RNA design by preserving the binding activities of both components.

papers.title: Lanosterol is the biosynthetic precursor of solanoeclepins, root-secreted hatching factors for potato cyst nematodes.
papers.abstract: Solanoeclepins are highly modified triterpenoids secreted from tomato and potato roots that act as potent hatching factors for potato cyst nematodes and are therefore important targets for the development of sustainable control strategies. However, their biosynthetic origin has remained unknown, limiting our understanding of their biological functions and practical exploitation. In this study, we identified the initial step of solanoeclepin biosynthesis using tomato hairy roots lacking lanosterol synthase, together with chemical complementation and stable isotope feeding experiments using deuterium-labeled lanosterol to validate its precursor role. Disruption of lanosterol synthase abolished lanosterol production and greatly reduced solanoeclepin accumulation. Exogenous lanosterol restored solanoeclepin production, and deuterium-labeled lanosterol was directly incorporated into solanoeclepins, providing definitive evidence that lanosterol is their biosynthetic precursor. Our results establish the entry point to the solanoeclepin biosynthesis and reveal a previously unrecognized function of plant lanosterol metabolism in the biosynthesis of root-secreted signaling molecules. These findings provide a foundation for elucidating the complete solanoeclepin biosynthetic pathway, exploring the biological roles of lanosterol-derived metabolites in plants, and enabling metabolic engineering approaches for sustainable potato cyst nematode control.

papers.title: Enzymatic strategies for PET valorization: Advances in discovery, engineering, and cyanobacterial chassis development.
papers.abstract: The global accumulation of plastic waste has intensified the need for sustainable technologies capable of replacing conventional mechanical and chemical recycling. During the past decade, enzymatic plastic biodegradation has rapidly evolved from the identification of individual depolymerases to an interdisciplinary research field integrating environmental microbiology, artificial intelligence, protein engineering, systems biology, and synthetic biology. Despite remarkable progress, current research remains largely fragmented, with enzyme discovery, catalytic optimization, and downstream plastic valorization often being developed independently, thereby limiting the establishment of integrated plastic biomanufacturing platforms. In this review, we critically synthesize advances in plastic-degrading enzymes, covering meta-omics and AI-assisted enzyme discovery, protein engineering strategies that improve catalytic efficiency, thermostability, and substrate specificity, and metabolic engineering approaches for assimilating plastic-derived monomers into value-added products. Rather than viewing these advances as separate research directions, we propose an integrated biotechnology framework that connects environmental enzyme mining, AI-driven protein engineering, microbial metabolic rewiring, and photosynthetic cell factories into a unified plastic-to-product strategy. Recent progress in heterologous protein secretion and metabolic engineering in cyanobacteria supports the continued exploration of solar-powered microbial platforms; however, complete PET-to-product bioconversion in cyanobacteria remains conceptual and has not yet been experimentally demonstrated. We anticipate that the convergence of multi-omics, artificial intelligence, enzyme engineering, and synthetic biology will shift the field from improving individual plastic-degrading enzymes toward constructing complete microbial plastic bioconversion systems, thereby accelerating the realization of a sustainable circular plastic bioeconomy.

papers.title: Metabolic engineering of Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) for plasmid-free high-level production of ergothioneine via hybrid pathway and multicopy chromosomal integration.
papers.abstract: Ergothioneine (L-ergothioneine, EGT) is an antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective compound with high value in the food, cosmeceutical, and nutraceutical industries. Herein, an efficient microbial cell factory was developed by engineering a hybrid EGT biosynthetic pathway in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) through the synergistic assembly of heterologous genetic modules of prokaryotic and eukaryotic origins. Systematic interrogation of gene combinations and transcriptional architectures identified sulfoxide synthase-mediated oxidative coupling as the pivotal metabolic bottleneck governing EGT biosynthetic flux. Addressing this rate-limiting step allowed the initial plasmid-bearing strain, EGT04, reaching an EGT titer of 156.35 mg/L during shake-flask fermentation. A multicopy chromosomal integration CRISPR-associated transposase strategy was implemented for stable multicopy chromosomal integration. This approach yielded a genetically robust, plasmid-free, and marker-free chassis, EGT15, which achieved an EGT titer of 287.14 mg/L, representing a 127.47% improvement over the initial prototype. Subsequent refinement of the fermentation landscape, integrating optimized glycerol feeding and strategic cysteine supplementation with a two-stage thermal control strategy (biomass accumulation at 37 °C followed by induction at 20 °C), further elevated the shake-flask titer to 353.69 mg/L. The final scale-up in a 5 L-fed-batch bioreactor culminated in a peak EGT concentration of 8.36 g/L with a volumetric productivity of 0.12 g/L/h. By eliminating the requirements for antibiotics and plasmid maintenance, this high-yielding and stable platform minimizes metabolic drag and enhances the industrial production potential. This study established a robust, plasmid-free, and resistance-free E. coli platform for sustainable microbial manufacturing of EGT, providing a scalable strategy for the high-level production of value-added sulfur-containing compounds.

papers.title: SynAb: Interpretable heavy-light chain synergy modeling for generalizable antibody-antigen interaction prediction.
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of antibody-antigen interactions (AAIs) is essential for therapeutic antibody discovery and high-throughput antibody screening. However, existing sequence-based methods often model antibody heavy and light chains independently, overlooking their cooperative contribution to antigen recognition. In this study, we propose SynAb, a synergy-guided cross-attention framework that integrates heavy-light chain regional cooperation into antibody-antigen interaction modeling. SynAb captures cooperative information across antibody functional regions and uses it to guide the interaction between antibody and antigen representations. Experimental results on the HIV and CoV-AbDab datasets demonstrate that SynAb outperforms the evaluated sequence-based methods and exhibits strong generalization in challenging scenarios involving unseen antibodies, unseen antigens, and previously unobserved antibody-antigen pairs. Beyond its predictive performance, SynAb explicitly characterizes the coordinated roles of paired heavy and light chains in antigen recognition. Moreover, without residue-level contact supervision, the model consistently highlights heavy-chain CDR-enriched regions, particularly CDR-H2 and CDR-H3, providing interpretable evidence consistent with established immunological knowledge. Together, these findings establish SynAb as a robust and interpretable framework for sequence-based AAI prediction and a promising computational tool for candidate prioritization in therapeutic antibody screening and synthetic biology applications.

papers.title: Navigating the Drought Tolerance-Yield Trade-Off in Triticeae Cereals: From Molecular Networks to Climate-Resilient Breeding.
papers.abstract: Drought driven by climate change severely threatens food security, particularly for wheat and barley grown in water-limited regions. A major breeding challenge is the trade-off between drought tolerance and yield. This review synthesises current knowledge of drought adaptation mechanisms in Triticeae crops, focusing on the transcriptional cascades, ABA-centric hormonal signalling and posttranslational modifications (kinases, phosphatases and ubiquitination) that confer resilience while often constraining carbon allocation to developing grains. Recent genomic advances, including genome-wide association study (GWAS), multi-omics integration and single-cell RNA-transcriptomics, have uncovered a wealth of drought-associated loci, although their translational potential is limited by data heterogeneity, environmental dependency and a persistent gap between laboratory validation and field performance. Emerging breeding approaches, such as speed breeding, wild-allele introgression, multiplex CRISPR/Cas9 and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven phenotyping are accelerating the development of climate-smart cultivars. Tissue-specific and inducible expression systems show early promise in uncoupling stress protection from growth penalties. Looking ahead, we propose that overcoming the yield-tolerance trade-off will require integrating synthetic biology, explainable AI, systematic exploration of novel variation and field phenomics coupled with digital twin modelling. Collectively, this review provides a strategic framework for engineering next-generation, climate-smart Triticeae cereals capable of maintaining productivity under intensifying drought conditions.

papers.title: Computable Genomes: A Layered Computational Framework for Non-Coding DNA and Cellular Behavior
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have catalogued tens of thousands of trait-associated loci, most of them in non-coding DNA, yet for most loci the path from nucleotide to phenotype remains correlational. We propose a layered computational decomposition of the genome as a complement to data-driven approaches: sequence as formal language, sequence as information-bearing signal, mobile elements as runtime, compilation to interaction networks through thermodynamic and rule-based models, and execution as cellular and multicellular dynamics. Each layer is defined by its inputs, outputs and formalisms, and we set out where the frame breaks down, including the looseness of algorithmic-information estimates, the triviality of universality results and the failure of string grammars at the chromatin level. Synthetic-biology platforms serve as tests of whether the layers compose, and genomic foundation models and the AlphaGenome Atlas, which predicts effects for all nine billion possible single-nucleotide variants, serve as oracles whose coverage and limits we map onto the framework. We state five falsifiable predictions and test the first, that sequence compressibility carries information about regulatory function beyond composition and conservation, on 38,556 single-nucleotide variants from a saturation-mutagenesis reporter assay of 21 regulatory elements. In a pooled model, local compressibility is associated with measured effect size (standardized β = −0.030, p = 0.0014). The association roughly halves under full control for base composition, loses significance when composition, motif and noise adjustments are combined under locus-level inference (wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.11), and averages zero within loci (random-effects β = −0.0003, p = 0.90). The prediction is therefore not supported at the variant level in these data, which bound the effect a genome-wide test should expect. The argument is not that the genome "is" a program, but that treating it as one supplies formal tools whose predictions can be checked.

papers.title: Reprogramming Protein Function by Expanding Chemical and Combinatorial Space: Integrating Chemical and Computational Strategies.
papers.abstract: Proteins are biological macromolecules that perform critical functions, including catalysis, molecular recognition, and cellular regulation. Natural evolution has generated remarkable protein diversity, leaving vast opportunities for engineered molecular innovation. Protein engineering has evolved from the rational design of proteins over the last few decades to approaches based on directed evolution and computational methods to enhance their properties. Protein engineering is shifting from optimization-based approaches to an integrated approach, which includes rational design, directed evolution, computational and generative modeling, synthetic chemistry, synthetic biology, and laboratory automation. These strategies widen the scope of experimentally accessible chemical and structural toolboxes in proteins without sacrificing the physicochemical constraints, cellular compatibility, evolutionary processes, and experimental validation. Meanwhile, synthetic chemistry is extending the natural abilities of proteins by incorporating noncanonical amino acids, novel cofactors, and modified metal centers and catalytic environments. These technologies enable the creation of artificial enzymes, programmed molecular binders, synthetic receptors, molecular machines, and biomaterials that have functions beyond those of their natural counterparts. This review introduces advances in the protein engineering field, from past methods of modifying proteins to present-day opportunities for generating proteins with artificial intelligence, and explains how the fields of computation, chemistry, and biology are driving the future of programmable proteins.

papers.title: Construction of cell factories, and multi-enzymatic and chemoenzymatic cascades to enable the efficient production of alkaloids.
papers.abstract: Covering: up to 2025Alkaloids constitute an invaluable reservoir for pharmaceutical discovery. However, their therapeutic development has long been constrained by the inefficiencies of plant extraction, as well as the economic impracticality of total chemical synthesis. In recent years, biomanufacturing has emerged as a transformative paradigm, enabling sustainable and scalable access to these complex molecules. This review provides an overview of the pivotal advances in alkaloid biosynthesis, delineated across de novo biosynthesis in prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems, concise multi-enzyme cascades, and chemoenzymatic synthesis. By discussing these pioneering examples, analyzing the strategic lessons, inherent limitations, and corresponding solutions for these platforms, this review illuminates how synthetic biology and biocatalysis are collectively reshaping the landscape of alkaloid production and paving the way for their expanded pharmaceutical applications.

papers.title: Lanosterol is the biosynthetic precursor of solanoeclepins, root-secreted hatching factors for potato cyst nematodes.
papers.abstract: Solanoeclepins are highly modified triterpenoids secreted from tomato and potato roots that act as potent hatching factors for potato cyst nematodes and are therefore important targets for the development of sustainable control strategies. However, their biosynthetic origin has remained unknown, limiting our understanding of their biological functions and practical exploitation. In this study, we identified the initial step of solanoeclepin biosynthesis using tomato hairy roots lacking lanosterol synthase, together with chemical complementation and stable isotope feeding experiments using deuterium-labeled lanosterol to validate its precursor role. Disruption of lanosterol synthase abolished lanosterol production and greatly reduced solanoeclepin accumulation. Exogenous lanosterol restored solanoeclepin production, and deuterium-labeled lanosterol was directly incorporated into solanoeclepins, providing definitive evidence that lanosterol is their biosynthetic precursor. Our results establish the entry point to the solanoeclepin biosynthesis and reveal a previously unrecognized function of plant lanosterol metabolism in the biosynthesis of root-secreted signaling molecules. These findings provide a foundation for elucidating the complete solanoeclepin biosynthetic pathway, exploring the biological roles of lanosterol-derived metabolites in plants, and enabling metabolic engineering approaches for sustainable potato cyst nematode control.

papers.title: Metabolic Engineering of Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) for Plasmid-Free High-Level Production of Ergothioneine via Hybrid Pathway and Multicopy Chromosomal Integration.
papers.abstract: Ergothioneine (L-ergothioneine, EGT) is an antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective compound with high value in the food, cosmeceutical, and nutraceutical industries. Herein, an efficient microbial cell factory was developed by engineering a hybrid EGT biosynthetic pathway in Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) through the synergistic assembly of heterologous genetic modules of prokaryotic and eukaryotic origins. Systematic interrogation of gene combinations and transcriptional architectures identified sulfoxide synthase-mediated oxidative coupling as the pivotal metabolic bottleneck governing EGT biosynthetic flux. Addressing this rate-limiting step allowed the initial plasmid-bearing strain, EGT04, reaching an EGT titer of 156.35mg/L during shake-flask fermentation. A multicopy chromosomal integration CRISPR-associated transposase strategy was implemented for stable multicopy chromosomal integration. This approach yielded a genetically robust, plasmid-free, and marker-free chassis, EGT15, which achieved an EGT titer of 287.14mg/L, representing a 127.47% improvement over the initial prototype. Subsequent refinement of the fermentation landscape, integrating optimized glycerol feeding and strategic cysteine supplementation with a two-stage thermal control strategy (biomass accumulation at 37 °C followed by induction at 20 °C), further elevated the shake-flask titer to 353.69mg/L. The final scale-up in a 5 L-fed-batch bioreactor culminated in a peak EGT concentration of 8.36g/L with a volumetric productivity of 0.12g/L/h. By eliminating the requirements for antibiotics and plasmid maintenance, this high-yielding and stable platform minimizes metabolic drag and enhances the industrial production potential. This study established a robust, plasmid-free, and resistance-free E. coli platform for sustainable microbial manufacturing of EGT, providing a scalable strategy for the high-level production of value-added sulfur-containing compounds.

papers.title: Continuous Concentration of an Enveloped Virus Using Multi-Pass Tangential Flow Filtration.
papers.abstract: Continuous biomanufacturing often offers increased productivity and reduced capital costs over batch processing. However, the concentration of biomolecules, a critical step for reducing volumetric load, remains a challenge. While single-pass tangential flow filtration (SPTFF) is designed for continuous workflows, the low feed flow rates often lead to membrane fouling and limited operational stability. In this study, we explore a continuous tangential flow filtration (cTFF) configuration as a robust alternative. The cTFF design utilizes a high flow rate circulation loop with a continuous input and output from the loop. This design decouples membrane crossflow velocity from the overall volumetric throughput, providing increased shear rates to minimize fouling, while maintaining continuous flows into and out of the system. Suid herpesvirus 1 (SuHV) was used as a surrogate enveloped virus to determine an operational space to achieve high recovery without viral titer loss. The configuration was subsequently integrated into a continuous production line for influenza virus-like particles (IA VLPs). The cTFF achieved an 8X volumetric concentration and maintained steady-state operation for 21 h. cTFF bridges the gap between the operational robustness of traditional batch recirculating TFF and the need for continuous bioprocessing, providing a scalable solution for continuous concentration.

papers.title: Enzymatic strategies for PET valorization: Advances in discovery, engineering, and cyanobacterial chassis development.
papers.abstract: The global accumulation of plastic waste has intensified the need for sustainable technologies capable of replacing conventional mechanical and chemical recycling. During the past decade, enzymatic plastic biodegradation has rapidly evolved from the identification of individual depolymerases to an interdisciplinary research field integrating environmental microbiology, artificial intelligence, protein engineering, systems biology, and synthetic biology. Despite remarkable progress, current research remains largely fragmented, with enzyme discovery, catalytic optimization, and downstream plastic valorization often being developed independently, thereby limiting the establishment of integrated plastic biomanufacturing platforms. In this review, we critically synthesize advances in plastic-degrading enzymes, covering meta-omics and AI-assisted enzyme discovery, protein engineering strategies that improve catalytic efficiency, thermostability, and substrate specificity, and metabolic engineering approaches for assimilating plastic-derived monomers into value-added products. Rather than viewing these advances as separate research directions, we propose an integrated biotechnology framework that connects environmental enzyme mining, AI-driven protein engineering, microbial metabolic rewiring, and photosynthetic cell factories into a unified plastic-to-product strategy. Recent progress in heterologous protein secretion and metabolic engineering in cyanobacteria supports the continued exploration of solar-powered microbial platforms; however, complete PET-to-product bioconversion in cyanobacteria remains conceptual and has not yet been experimentally demonstrated. We anticipate that the convergence of multi-omics, artificial intelligence, enzyme engineering, and synthetic biology will shift the field from improving individual plastic-degrading enzymes toward constructing complete microbial plastic bioconversion systems, thereby accelerating the realization of a sustainable circular plastic bioeconomy.

papers.title: Microliter to liter scale engineering of cell-free 1,2,4-butanetriol biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: Biomanufacturing offers sustainable alternatives to traditional chemical synthesis under milder temperatures and pressures. However, the slow pace and iterative engineering bottlenecks of cell strain development restrict the feasible biological design space. Cell-free systems circumvent these constraints, providing a flexible and high-throughput screening approach to accelerate pathway prototyping and enzyme optimization, yet they are not typically used for manufacturing scale-up. To evaluate the scalability of cell-free biosynthesis, we establish an end-to-end fully cell-free architecture to discover, develop, and scale the biosynthesis of 1,2,4-butanetriol (BT), a high-value industrial platform chemical. First, we systematically screened ∼150 enzymes across the 4-step pathway from xylose to BT to identify highly active homologs for each reaction. Next, we applied statistical Design of Experiments to optimize reaction formulations for cost and titer. Finally, the maximum-titer and minimum-cost formulations were scaled up across five orders of magnitude, from 10 μL to 1 L reactions. This resulted in peak volumetric productivities of ∼1 g/L/h and titers over 13 g of BT in a single 1 L reaction, with reagent costs totaling just $3.00 per liter. This work expands the diversity of enzymes tested for BT synthesis and establishes a blueprint for advancing industrial biochemical manufacturing fully in vitro, opening future opportunities for bioreactor integration with continuous or fed-batch operation and online product recovery.

papers.title: Engineering signal transduction for closed-loop gene and cell therapies.
papers.abstract: Chronic diseases are still treated largely with interventions that are constitutive, intermittently administered and poorly aligned with real-time physiology. Synthetic biology is changing this paradigm by treating gene circuits as programmable genetic software that can be deployed across cellular therapeutic hardware spanning from prokaryotic to eukaryotic systems, including probiotic cells, designer cells, immune cells and stem‑cell‑derived platforms. In this framework, engineered systems can sense disease-associated signals, compute them through synthetic or repurposed transduction pathways and adjust therapeutic output to maintain physiological variables within a desired range. Closed-loop therapeutics therefore begin to merge diagnosis, treatment and prevention within the same living platform. Across metabolism, inflammation, infection, cardiovascular regulation and cancer, early mammalian systems show that endogenous sensing, intracellular computation and therapeutic actuation can be combined in clinically relevant architectures. The emerging concept of setpoint medicine captures the clinical ambition of these systems: not simply to deliver a dose, but to keep physiology within an interpretable and therapeutically desirable range. Realizing this vision will require durable and modular control circuits, hardware-aware delivery strategies, interpretable safety frameworks, controller-style performance metrics and increasingly AI-assisted design, calibration and oversight. If these challenges can be met, the future of therapy may be defined less by intermittent dosing than by the continuous control of physiology.

papers.title: Targeted design of next-generation electroactive microorganisms.
papers.abstract: Bioelectrochemical systems (BESs) convert chemical energy into electrical energy or vice versa by utilizing microorganisms. Early proof-of-concept studies employed wild-type electroactive microorganisms (EAMs) that can exchange electrons with external acceptors such as electrodes, a process called extracellular electron transfer (EET). However, wild-type EAMs are limited by modest performance, restricted product spectra, and complex process control. A deeper understanding of the molecular EET mechanisms has allowed a targeted enhancement of BES processes. Advances in genetic and metabolic engineering have enabled increased electron transfer rates, redox pathway rewiring, and broader product spectra, expanding the potential of BESs by generating engineered, next-generation EAMs (ngEAMs). This review outlines recent advances and strategies for target identification and for process-tailored, ngEAMs, and their application in processes of high interest to biotechnology.

papers.title: Differential and Cooperative Immunomodulation by Saponin Adjuvants QS-21 and QS-7 in Human THP-1 Macrophages
papers.abstract: QS-21, a triterpene glycoside saponin derived from Quillaja saponaria, is a potent immunostimulatory adjuvant incorporated in several FDA-approved vaccines. QS-7, a structurally related saponin fraction, has been reported to retain immunomodulatory activity with reduced hemolytic toxicity; however, its lower natural abundance has limited its systematic immunological characterization. To address this gap, we systematically compare responses to QS-21 and QS-7 in the THP-1 human macrophage model to resolve their distinct and cooperative contributions to antigen presenting cell (APC) activation. Following cytotoxicity profiling to establish safe and biologically relevant dosing, flow cytometry, proteomics, and transcriptomics were used to delineate the immunological programs engaged by each saponin alone and in combination. QS-7 alone induced minimal upregulation of cell surface activation markers and did not elicit a significant transcriptional signature, yet it drove dose-dependent secretion of a broad panel of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, revealing a dissociation between these two arms of macrophage activation. Strikingly, co-administration of QS-7 with QS-21 substantially potentiated macrophage activation across all parameters tested, amplifying surface marker upregulation, broadening cytokine and chemokine output to include IL-12p70 and IFN-γ, and markedly expanding the pro-inflammatory transcriptional and pathway landscape induced by QS-21, while concurrently suppressing counter-regulatory lipid-sensing pathways (PPAR, RAR, FXR/RXR) that constrain inflammatory output. Collectively, these findings establish QS-7 not merely as an attenuated analog of QS-21, but as a functionally distinct immunomodulator that recalibrates both the magnitude and regulatory tone of QS-21-driven macrophage activation. These findings show that structurally distinct saponins elicit distinct and complementary macrophage responses, providing a foundation for structure-function studies. Together with synthetic biology and data-driven design, this knowledge can guide the development of new-to-nature saponin adjuvants.

papers.title: Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase bifunctionally catalyzes ring formation involving sequential terminal carbon oxidation for pyrrolizidinone alkaloid biosynthesis.
papers.abstract: The Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase UcsF plays a key role in the early biosynthesis of UCS1025A, an antibacterial and antitumor pyrrolizidinone alkaloid, by participating in the formation of its core ring scaffold. UcsF catalyzes sequential oxidation of the terminal C5 of L-isoleucine, ultimately generating a five-membered ring product, (2S,3S)-3,4-dihydro-3-methyl-2H-pyrrole-2-carboxylic acid. This catalytic process is vital in the construction of natural product skeletons and synthetic biology. However, the molecular basis of UcsF and its unique two-step catalytic mechanism remain poorly understood. papers.title: Empirical optimization of dCas12a-based CRISPRi/a for pooled screening in Yarrowia lipolytica

papers.title: Beyond the Primary-Secondary Dichotomy: Toward a Unified Metabolic Perspective.
papers.abstract: The distinction between primary and secondary metabolism has long provided a useful conceptual and pedagogical framework in biochemistry, particularly in plant sciences, but it increasingly fails as a literal description of how metabolites are produced and function. Pathways share precursors, cofactors, regulatory mechanisms, transport systems, and recycling routes, while metabolites conventionally assigned to different categories can contribute to growth, signaling, defense, nutrient acquisition, structure, or stress responses depending on context. We do not argue that established terms must be abolished: they remain useful descriptors of broad tendencies in conservation, distribution, and pathway organization. Instead, we argue against treating them as fixed functional categories. We develop an operational framework in which network position, flux and resource coupling, phylogenetic distribution, spatiotemporal localization, conditional essentiality, and experimentally demonstrated function are evaluated together. We then show how this perspective changes the analysis of untargeted metabolomic data and the design of metabolic-engineering strategies. A unified metabolic perspective provides a practical way to connect plant physiology, environmental responses, and ecological interactions without replacing established terminology with a new rigid vocabulary.

papers.title: Chromosome-level genomics and cross-species enzyme screening enable high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica
papers.abstract: The diversity of enzymes supporting bakuchiol biosynthesis remains incompletely characterized, limiting the repertoire available for microbial pathway engineering. Here, we combined chromosome-level genomics, cross-species enzyme screening and metabolic engineering to establish high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica. We assembled a 471.76-Mb Psoralea corylifolia genome anchored to 11 pseudochromosomes, with a contig N50 of 40.33 Mb. Genome-guided screening and functional validation identified four prenyltransferases from P. corylifolia and Vigna radiata whose N-terminally truncated variants supported bakuchiol production in yeast. These results extend experimental evidence for bakuchiol-producing activity across legume prenyltransferase sequences and species. Coordinating mevalonate pathway reinforcement with increased t40PcPT6 gene dosage further improved bakuchiol production. These findings connect an expanded set of functional prenyltransferases with coordinated pathway engineering, enabling gram-per-liter microbial bakuchiol production.

papers.title: Cell-free protein synthesis for next-generation biomanufacturing.
papers.abstract: Chemicals with diverse molecular structures are essential to the pharmaceutical, food, and specialty chemical industries; however, their sustainable production remains challenging due to complex cellular regulation, limited metabolic flexibility, and the scalability constraints of purified enzyme-based systems. Extract-based cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) has emerged as a versatile biomanufacturing platform that enables the production of functional enzymes in vitro and provides an open, programmable environment for constructing synthetic biosynthetic systems beyond the constraints of living cells. By decoupling chemical synthesis from cellular growth, CFPS allows precise control over enzyme composition, pathway stoichiometry, and cofactor utilization, thereby improving catalytic efficiency and resource utilization. In this review, we summarize recent advances in extract-based CFPS for chemical biosynthesis and discuss key engineering strategies, including cofactor regeneration, pathway balancing, and semicontinuous operation, to enhance system performance. Furthermore, we highlight emerging opportunities to integrate CFPS with artificial intelligence-guided design, renewable feedstocks, and modular reactor technologies toward more sustainable and scalable biomanufacturing processes.

papers.title: On-demand biomanufacturing via programmed SporeBot.
papers.abstract: Biopharmaceuticals, including antimicrobial peptides and engineered protein-based vaccines, represent key products of the biotechnology sector. However, their reliance on large-scale manufacturing and cold-chain logistics limits deployment in field and resource-limited settings. To address this gap, we developed SporeBot, a platform that exploits the intrinsic stability of Bacillus subtilis spores for versatile and on-demand biopharmaceutical production. The platform comprises polymeric microcapsules that encapsulate engineered spores. These spores exhibit robust stability, retaining engineered functionality under harsh conditions and extended storage. Upon activation, germinated cells secrete the target proteins, which diffuse across a polymeric mesh that physically separates the cellular factory from the secreted product. We validate this platform through the production and functional testing of antimicrobial peptides and vaccine antigens. Our approach resolves key manufacturing and distribution constraints of protein therapeutics and offers a deployable solution for on-demand biomanufacturing in both developed and resource-limited settings.

papers.title: Hierarchical design strategies for tuning genetic circuits.
papers.abstract: Genetic circuit design is central to synthetic biology, yet achieving predictable and programmable circuit performance remains challenging due to diverse circuit- and host-dependent factors. Thus, a systematic perspective is needed to integrate these factors across multiple design layers. In this review, we establish a hierarchical framework for tuning genetic circuits as an engineering process spanning biological part design, DNA synthesis and assembly, carrier selection, host-cell implementation, and cross-host transfer. We further discuss how each layer contributes to circuit behavior and shapes trade-offs among key performance properties. By integrating hierarchical design strategies with iterative troubleshooting, this review provides a practical roadmap for tuning genetic circuits toward more predictable and reliable performance.

papers.title: Efficient Bioproduction of Citric Acid in Aspergillus niger.
papers.abstract: Citric acid is the most widely produced organic acid in industrial biotechnology, with a global annual output exceeding 2 million tons and broad applications across the food, pharmaceutical, chemical, and environmental sectors. Despite more than a century of industrial development since the discovery of citric acid fermentation by Aspergillus niger in 1917, current production systems are approaching critical bottlenecks in strain performance, process efficiency, and environmental sustainability. Increasing evidence indicates that citrate overproduction is not governed by a single metabolic pathway but emerges as a multi-constraint-driven systems phenomenon involving coordinated regulation of metabolism, cellular physiology, and environmental conditions. Recent advances in systems biology and synthetic biology have enabled a paradigm shift from empirical optimization to rational and programmable biomanufacturing. The integration of multi-omics data with genome-scale metabolic models has substantially deepened the understanding of citrate overflow metabolism. In parallel, the development of CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editing, dynamic gene regulation systems, and promoter engineering has enabled precise and multiplexed rewiring of metabolic networks. Targeted engineering strategies focusing on carbon uptake, mitochondrial metabolism, citrate transport, and morphology regulation have demonstrated that high-level production requires coordinated multi-layer optimization rather than single-gene modifications. At the process level, emerging strategies, including immobilized fermentation, in situ product recovery, and the utilization of alternative non-food feedstocks, are being increasingly integrated with engineered strains to enhance productivity and sustainability. These advances collectively point toward a transition from conventional fermentation to a multi-scale, integrated biomanufacturing framework. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent progress in citric acid biomanufacturing, covering the evolution of industrial A. niger strains, systems-level mechanisms of citrate accumulation, synthetic biology-enabled tool development, rational chassis engineering strategies, and process intensification approaches. Finally, we discuss future directions, including dynamic metabolic control, artificial intelligence-assisted design, and circular biorefinery systems, aiming to establish a fully integrated, intelligent, and sustainable paradigm for next-generation citric acid production.

papers.title: Targeting bacterial signaling pathways: a paradigm shift in antimicrobial strategies for food safety.
papers.abstract: Foodborne bacterial contamination represents a critical challenge to global food safety and public health. Pathogenic bacteria cause millions of foodborne illnesses annually, while spoilage organisms lead to substantial economic losses through product deterioration. Nearly one in ten people worldwide contract foodborne illnesses each year, resulting in approximately 420,000 deaths annually. US$ 110 billion is lost each year in productivity and medical expenses resulting from unsafe food in low and middle-income countries. Conventional preservation methods face limitations including quality degradation, residual toxicity, and growing consumer demand for clean-label solutions. Bacterial signaling pathways orchestrate virulence, biofilm formation, and stress adaptation, offering novel anti-virulence targets that preserve food quality while minimizing microbial hazards. This review systematically examines three major bacterial signaling pathways as novel targets for food antimicrobial strategies. Emerging intervention platforms are evaluated, including computational biology, nanotechnology, synthetic biology, natural QS inhibitors, and enzymatic degradation strategies, with emphasis on practical applications in cold chain, fermented foods, and meat products. Targeting signaling pathways demonstrates significant potential for controlling pathogens. Key challenges include signal molecule stability in food matrices, bioavailability optimization. Multi-target intervention strategies combining computational screening, natural inhibitors, and engineered delivery systems represent the most promising direction for next-generation food antimicrobials.

papers.title: Diffusion integrity testing of small-area sterilizing-grade membrane filters in single-use assemblies.
papers.abstract: Sterile filtration represents the final critical step in biomanufacturing, where a sterilizing-grade membrane filter removes microbial contamination from the drug product - making filter integrity verification essential. While bubble point and gas-liquid diffusion tests are established non-destructive methods for hydrophilic membranes, diffusion testing offers high sensitivity to small defects and operates at lower test pressures. However, applying diffusion testing to small-area filters integrated into closed single-use assemblies remains challenging because pressure changes measured by automated integrity testers can arise not only from membrane diffusion, but also from assembly-related effects such as gas-permeable tubing, upstream volume and thermal equilibration. For low-area devices, these background contributions can become comparable to or greater than the membrane signal, reducing test sensitivity and complicating interpretation. This work presents a practical method for implementing diffusion-based integrity testing of small-format sterilizing-grade filters in final sealed single-use assemblies. The approach quantifies assembly-specific background contribution and incorporates it into an adjusted diffusion specification, allowing membrane-specific diffusion to be resolved without altering the assembled system. By accounting for system-derived measurement noise, the method enables reliable end-user integrity assessment of closed assemblies that cannot be reconfigured to reduce upstream volume or replace high-permeability tubing materials.

papers.title: Physiological, behavioral, and genetic factors that shape interactions in the plant growth-promoting maize rhizosphere synthetic community.
papers.abstract: Profiling microbiomes is an important way to understand the function and composition of communities in the wild, but natural microbiomes are often highly complex and often unamenable to experimentation to reveal cause-and-effect relationships. By using a small group of cultivable strains to represent those found in the wild, synthetic communities are one solution to this problem. Here we describe the ma ize r hizosphere s ynthetic c ommunity (MARSc), a genome-enabled 31-member bacterial community representative of the diversity found on the roots of maize grown in Iowa soils. This community is built around Pseudomonas putida KT2440, a model maize rhizosphere colonist and synthetic biology chassis. We characterized microbe-microbe interactions and biofilm formation of MARSc members in a variety of environmental contexts, finding that both behaviors are broadly controlled by nutrient levels. Genomic analysis and microbiome profiling of these organisms revealed that annotated biofilm genes (such as surface attachment and exopolysaccharide production) were significantly correlated with rhizosphere abundance, but neither trait correlated to in vitro biofilm formation. In vitro interaction assay findings were surprisingly consistent with co-correlations of rhizosphere abundance among MARSc members on roots. Finally, we found that when applied to the roots, MARSc can increase maize biomass (dry weight) by up to 40%-50% under varying nitrogen fertilization levels. Altogether, MARSc is a useful tool for identifying some of the factors influencing rhizosphere microbiome assembly and will be a strong foundation for further work in this area.IMPORTANCEThe microbiome surrounding the roots of plants can play an integral role in plant health and growth, and it is composed of thousands of species of microbes that are specific to the plant and environment it is grown in. However, due to this complexity, little is known about the means by which microbiomes form. In this study, we developed the maize rhizosphere synthetic community (MARSc) to gain a better understanding of the formation and function of microbiomes on the roots of plants. papers.title: Chloroplast genome engineering: Recent advances, pathways towards commercialization and future directions.
papers.abstract: Chloroplasts are ideal biofactories because thousands of transgene copies integrated into each plant cell to produce high levels of recombinant proteins and enzymes. Because chloroplast genomes are predominantly maternally inherited, transgenes are generally not transmitted via pollen. Nuclear genome engineering ushered in the GMO revolution for crop protection that mostly required lower levels of transgene expression. Higher level expression and biosafety through gene containment facilitate new applications of GM crops, including production of high-value biopharmaceuticals and enzymes. This review focuses on recent advances in this field, including the first FDA approval of biopharmaceuticals made in plant cells for evaluation in human clinical trials, topical or oral drug delivery, marker free edible plants by removal of antibiotic resistance genes and novel post-translational modifications required to produce functional human proteins. In addition, new tools are discussed to improve DNA delivery, vector free assembly, episomal or integration methods, enhancement of transgene expression through optimization of regulatory sequences, codons, targeted genome editing and other innovations in biomanufacturing. Topical drug delivery using plant cells incorporated into chewing gums to control oral viruses, pathogenic bacteria, or yeast and oral drug delivery with therapeutic proteins made in plant cells to treat diabetes, obesity and cardiopulmonary diseases currently advanced to human clinical trials are discussed. In addition, high-value industrial enzymes for launching new products or to confer valuable agronomic traits or enhance photosynthesis are discussed. Future perspectives section provides examples of biotechnology products anticipated to be launched in the next 3-5 years, with opportunities and anticipated challenges.

papers.title: Cell culture tightrope: Balancing amino acids and dipeptides to optimize media formulation and biomanufacturing performance.
papers.abstract: High-quality cell culture media remain central to mammalian bioprocessing as industry produces increasingly complex molecules at higher cell densities under intensified processing conditions. Amino acids represent a critical class of media components, serving as building blocks for endogenous and recombinant proteins and also as key regulators of cellular metabolism. This requires delivery of amino acids at concentrations that challenge their stability and solubility limits. This review provides an overview of amino acid roles in cell culture and how to choose their optimal levels in media formulations, with a focus on Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. Omics-assisted medium development strategies are described to characterize amino acid metabolism and minimize metabolic inefficiencies arising from amino acid degradation. Additionally, genetic engineering approaches aimed at introducing amino acid auxotrophies or removing metabolic bottlenecks are discussed as complementary strategies to improve cell culture performance. Understanding the physicochemical limitations associated with amino acid solubility becomes increasingly important in concentrated media formulations. Emerging in silico thermodynamic models that capture interactions between amino acids and other media components are highlighted as valuable tools for predicting solubility limits and guiding rational media formulation strategies. Dipeptides represent an increasingly attractive alternative to free amino acids due to improved solubility, stability, and process-enhancing properties. Consequently, this review summarizes key dipeptides, current knowledge of their uptake and metabolism, and the amino acid and dipeptide transporters and cleavage enzymes. Finally, the review emphasizes the importance of smart media design by integrating experiments with modeling approaches to enable efficient, robust, and sustainable biomanufacturing processes.

papers.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux.
papers.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.
papers.authors: Son SH, Bae S, Moon SY, Kim M, Oh SS, Son CY, Lee JY.

papers.title: Chloroplast genome engineering: Recent advances, pathways towards commercialization and future directions.
papers.abstract: Chloroplasts are ideal biofactories because thousands of transgene copies integrated into each plant cell to produce high levels of recombinant proteins and enzymes. Because chloroplast genomes are predominantly maternally inherited, transgenes are generally not transmitted via pollen. Nuclear genome engineering ushered in the GMO revolution for crop protection that mostly required lower levels of transgene expression. Higher level expression and biosafety through gene containment facilitate new applications of GM crops, including production of high-value biopharmaceuticals and enzymes. This review focuses on recent advances in this field, including the first FDA approval of biopharmaceuticals made in plant cells for evaluation in human clinical trials, topical or oral drug delivery, marker free edible plants by removal of antibiotic resistance genes and novel post-translational modifications required to produce functional human proteins. In addition, new tools are discussed to improve DNA delivery, vector free assembly, episomal or integration methods, enhancement of transgene expression through optimization of regulatory sequences, codons, targeted genome editing and other innovations in biomanufacturing. Topical drug delivery using plant cells incorporated into chewing gums to control oral viruses, pathogenic bacteria, or yeast and oral drug delivery with therapeutic proteins made in plant cells to treat diabetes, obesity and cardiopulmonary diseases currently advanced to human clinical trials are discussed. In addition, high-value industrial enzymes for launching new products or to confer valuable agronomic traits or enhance photosynthesis are discussed. Future perspectives section provides examples of biotechnology products anticipated to be launched in the next 3-5 years, with opportunities and anticipated challenges.
papers.authors: Fatima I, Daniell H.

papers.title: Cell culture tightrope: Balancing amino acids and dipeptides to optimize media formulation and biomanufacturing performance.
papers.abstract: High-quality cell culture media remain central to mammalian bioprocessing as industry produces increasingly complex molecules at higher cell densities under intensified processing conditions. Amino acids represent a critical class of media components, serving as building blocks for endogenous and recombinant proteins and also as key regulators of cellular metabolism. This requires delivery of amino acids at concentrations that challenge their stability and solubility limits. This review provides an overview of amino acid roles in cell culture and how to choose their optimal levels in media formulations, with a focus on Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. Omics-assisted medium development strategies are described to characterize amino acid metabolism and minimize metabolic inefficiencies arising from amino acid degradation. Additionally, genetic engineering approaches aimed at introducing amino acid auxotrophies or removing metabolic bottlenecks are discussed as complementary strategies to improve cell culture performance. Understanding the physicochemical limitations associated with amino acid solubility becomes increasingly important in concentrated media formulations. Emerging in silico thermodynamic models that capture interactions between amino acids and other media components are highlighted as valuable tools for predicting solubility limits and guiding rational media formulation strategies. Dipeptides represent an increasingly attractive alternative to free amino acids due to improved solubility, stability, and process-enhancing properties. Consequently, this review summarizes key dipeptides, current knowledge of their uptake and metabolism, and the amino acid and dipeptide transporters and cleavage enzymes. Finally, the review emphasizes the importance of smart media design by integrating experiments with modeling approaches to enable efficient, robust, and sustainable biomanufacturing processes.

papers.title: Global health security and smallpox: A strategic review of post-eradication biosafety and preparedness.
papers.abstract: The global biosecurity framework faces a potential critical transition driven by synthetic biology advancements and declining population-level immunity. This review evaluates smallpox as a central case study for contemporary pathogen governance and biopolitical preparedness. We analyze the convergence of two primary risks: the technical feasibility of de novo orthopoxvirus synthesis and the expanding immunity gap following the cessation of routine vaccination. The 2022 mpox resurgence is assessed as a sentinel event revealing strategic vulnerabilities in cross-protective immunity. Ultimately, this perspective argues that smallpox reemergence risk is not merely a technological byproduct, but a fundamental global governance crisis. To mitigate these threats, we propose a multidimensional framework integrated with One Health principles and transnational coordination. Maintaining strategic vigilance and institutional memory is presented as a critical political capacity for post-eradication health security.
